news.title: Anthropic mathematician claims AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis
paras: The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It proposes an origin for the prime numbers, namely that they follow a certain pattern. The question is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, which will award a $1 million prize for an accepted solution.

Levent Alpöge at Anthropic published a statement today claiming to have solved the problem with the aid of Anthropic’s Claude AI. “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” writes Alpöge. Alpöge hasn’t published a human-readable version of the proof, saying it would be “obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop'”, though he says an unpublished version ran to more than 250,000 pages.

news.title: Science has a home here at Ars—please help keep it that way
paras: Science has a home here at Ars—please help keep it that way Your support for Ars matters more now than ever. It has been the only home I’ve known as a writer, and it has been essential to my development from scientist to blogger to journalist.

news.title: I got to tour SpaceX's Starfactory facility in Starbase, Texas, and what I saw blew my mind
paras: For some context, the five-story-tall Starfactory spans approximately 1 million square feet (~93,000 meters), with operations split between Starship's Super Heavy boosters and upper stage Ships, and nearly 330,000 additional square feet (30,000 square meters) of office space. SpaceX officials describe its design as one more akin to an automotive manufacturing plant than that of a typical aerospace production site, and inside, it is absolutely alive with activity.
We entered through an arch-covered doorway underneath the giant "X" sign on the building's shorter face. Inside, we were struck with the sheer enormity of Starship's scale.

news.title: Nine-Pound Eagles Seem to Be Hunting 60-Pound Baboons in Africa—Hinting the Predators May Have Gone After Our
paras: Add as preferred source Researchers found talon marks on the remains of olive baboons. Catherine Hobaiter Eagles are formidable aerial predators capable of taking down animals much larger than themselves, including primates.

But scientists have long believed that eagles tend to go after smaller primates, generally weighing less than 30 pounds. Scientists have found evidence of Verreaux’s eagles hunting full-grown olive baboons weighing nearly 60 pounds, which they describe in a study published November 18 in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology . The findings add to scientists’ understanding of predator-prey relationships.

news.title: Dutch Elm Disease Virtually Wiped Out America's Most Iconic Tree. Now, Scientists Are Engineering a Comeback f
paras: Bernadette Osborn/The Nature Conservancy Vermont In some ways, Leila Wilson’s idyllic relationship with the American elm is a familiar story. “We had a big elm on the hill of our driveway that we put a tire swing on when I was a kid,” says the U.S. Forest Service research ecologist, recalling her childhood home outside of New Haven, which is known as Elm City.

Countless grandparents have a similar story to tell. What’s unique about Wilson’s recollection is the timing. Her childhood memories date back to the 1980s, and by then millions of American elms were gone—already felled by a fungus.

paras: Carlos Alcaraz refused to reveal his diagnosis on Friday in Turin, a day after an MRI that had put his ATP Finals in doubt. Asked what exactly he had and how risky it was, he said in Spanish: “Obviously I’m not going to say it here.
